Koch snowflake and a hand-drawn Escher-style tessellation.

Goal: I can describe the symmetries in a pattern.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html:
A tessellation covers the plane with shapes and no gaps or overlaps. Only three regular polygons tile the plane alone: triangles, squares and hexagons, because only their angles (60, 90, 120) divide 360 evenly.

Change one side of a square tile and slide the same change onto the opposite side, and the new tile still tiles by translation, as in Escher's designs. The initial equilateral triangle has 3 reflection axes and smallest positive rotation 120 degrees. The standard Koch snowflake from stage 1 onward, and in the limit, has 6 reflection axes and smallest positive rotation 60 degrees.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html: Why can't regular pentagons tile the plane?
slides.reveal: Each angle is 108 degrees, and 360 is not a multiple of 108, so the corners leave a gap or overlap.
